title: Judge gives Google one week to fix "anticompetitive" app store download in Google Play
gist: US District Judge James Donato found that Google's first implementation of court-mandated third-party app store distribution inside the Play Store added 'anticompetitive friction' — burying the landing page, suppressing search results for 'app store' and 'aptoide', and replacing the install button with a 'view' button — and gave Google one week to fix it. Aptoide Games is currently the only alternative store in Play, with Epic potentially next.

insights.claim: US District Judge James Donato reviewed Google's live implementation of third-party app store distribution inside the Play Store, ruled it added unnecessary 'anticompetitive friction', and gave Google one week to fix the identified issues.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: A judge auditing UI flows on a one-week clock means compliance risk for platform gatekeepers is now measured in weeks, not appeal cycles.
insights.quote: That has to be fixed. I want every possible variation that’s even only 70 percent properly phrased.
insights.locator: Google's lawyers contended in the hearing

insights.claim: Google lost the Epic antitrust case in 2023 and the years since have been consumed by determining how remedies get implemented, showing that in platform antitrust the remedy design phase — not the liability verdict — determines the economic outcome.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Model the multi-year remedy phase, not the verdict date, when pricing antitrust risk into platform revenue lines.

insights.claim: Epic's lawyer Yonatan Even demonstrated in court that Play Store searches for 'app store' and 'aptoide' return no direct results, instead showing only an 'are you looking for' banner linking to the third-party app store page.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Search suppression is the cheapest and least visible way a platform can nullify a distribution remedy; it is the compliance vector regulators will now check first.
insights.locator: While there is a link to the Play Store's alternative app store page

insights.claim: Google's third-party app store landing page is buried several levels deep in Play Store menus rather than being surfaced directly, which the court treated as deliberate friction rather than a design oversight.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Discovery depth is the real determinant of whether alternative distribution ever gains share; a mandated store nobody can find has near-zero revenue impact.
insights.locator: While there is a link to the Play Store's alternative app store page

insights.claim: Alternative app store listings in Play carried a 'view' button that opened an additional install dialog instead of the normal 'install' button, and Donato ordered the button changed to 'install' as the extra step appeared designed to discourage downloads.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Single-tap versus two-tap install is a measurable conversion difference; this is where the ruling actually changes installed-base economics for rival stores.
insights.locator: Another problem is the process of actually installing the store

insights.claim: Google's defense was that app stores warrant a special category because of their expanded permissions and that Epic had already conceded this, justifying the extra install step — an argument the court rejected.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Security framing is the standard platform defense against distribution remedies; its failure here weakens that line of defense for platform owners generally.
insights.quote: The court didn’t buy that explanation, though.
insights.locator: Google's lawyers contended in the hearing

themes.theme: Revealed preferences and what comes next

insights.claim: Google actively attempted to settle with Epic specifically to keep third-party app stores out of the Play Store, revealing that it values excluding rival stores more than settling the litigation.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Google's own revealed preference is the best estimate of how much Play Store economics are at stake — larger than the settlement value it was willing to pay.
insights.quote: Google worked hard to avoid this outcome, attempting to settle with Epic to keep third-party app stores out.
insights.locator: However, Google worked hard to avoid this outcome

insights.claim: Epic and Google are simultaneously patching things up through a global partnership agreement while remaining adversaries in the US antitrust case, so cooperation elsewhere does not blunt Epic's enforcement pressure in the US.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Don't read the partnership headline as antitrust de-risking; the US remedy track is proceeding independently.
insights.locator: While Epic and Google are patching things up

insights.claim: Aptoide Games is the first and currently only third-party store admitted to the Play Store under the ruling, leaving alternative Android distribution dependent on a single small operator for now.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Concentration in one store means the remedy's near-term commercial impact on Google's take rate is negligible until larger stores enter.
insights.locator: It's possible that once this process is complete

insights.claim: Once the install flow is fixed, Epic may finally release its own storefront inside Google Play, capitalizing on the ruling it spent years pursuing.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: An Epic storefront inside Play would be the first real test of whether mandated alternative distribution can take meaningful share from Google's billing take rate.
